title: The arrow-maker's fire
hookLine: at Devadaha: the fletcher warms the arrow to straighten it, then stops; effort without self-torment

cards: There are two ways to get nowhere with self-improvement. One is to never try.
The other is to try so hard you punish yourself: the 5am alarm you hate, the diet that makes you miserable, the inner voice that never says well done. The Buddha knew the second way well.

Before his awakening, the old stories say, he starved himself until he was skin and bone. In a Sakyan town called Devadaha, he talks about effort, and he reaches for a picture from a craftsman's workshop.

teach.b: The sutta opens with a debate about ascetics of the time who held that painful austerities burn away past actions. The Buddha questions that view at length. Then he describes what fruitful effort looks like.
A monk, he says, doesn't overwhelm himself with suffering. He doesn't reject a pleasure that's in line with the teaching, and he isn't infatuated with it either. Then the picture.
An arrow-maker has a crooked arrow shaft.
He warms it between two flames, turning it, heating it, bending it until it's straight and workable.
And once it's straight? He stops. He doesn't keep heating a straight arrow; the purpose is done.
In the same way, the Buddha says, a person might notice: when I live just as I please, unwholesome things grow in me; when I put in some hard effort, they fade.
So they apply the heat, as much as is needed, and when the purpose is achieved, they stop. Heat has a job: straightening. Harm has no job.
Self-punishment that goes on after the arrow is straight isn't discipline. It's just burning. The Dhammapada uses the same craftsman.
In Max Müller's words: "As a fletcher makes straight his arrow, a wise man makes straight his trembling and unsteady thought, which is difficult to guard, difficult to hold back."

teach.h: THE FLETCHER IS PATIENT WITH THE WOOD.
teach.b: The fletcher isn't angry at the wood.
He's patient with it, and he knows when to put the arrow down.

how: Buddhist teachers often describe the path as a middle way between indulgence and self-torment, and encourage steady, balanced effort in meditation rather than forcing.

o: a hunter who shoots with a bow
a crooked arrow that must be heated

p: as much as needed, then stop
the Sakyan town of the sutta

s: the sutta says a monk should reject every pleasure
he doesn't reject a pleasure in line with the teaching, nor is he infatuated with it.
the arrow-maker keeps heating the arrow after it's straight
once it's straight he stops: the purpose is done.
the Dhammapada also compares a wise person to a fletcher
in Müller's words, the wise man 'makes straight his trembling and unsteady thought.'

games.q: you're an arrow-maker. the shaft you've been heating is finally straight. what do you do?
o: heat it more, to be safe
games.why: he stops. the Buddha says effort works the same way: apply it as long as it straightens something, then put it down.

practice: Think of one thing in yourself you're working to straighten, a temper, a habit, a way of speaking, and notice how you usually talk to yourself about it: is it heat, or harm?
Picture the fletcher warming the shaft gently, turning it, checking it, and bring that tone to your own effort. Then rest with the breath, and let the heat go out.

wordCard.voice: Usukara. The fletcher heats a crooked shaft until it's straight, and then stops. Effort with a purpose, without self-torment.

orig.note: Pali usukāra: arrow-maker, fletcher. the craftsman in both this sutta and the Dhammapada.

carryVoice: Your line: heat, not harm. Once the arrow is straight, the heat has done its job. Day four hundred seventy-eight.
